description: We are Build Better Worlds, a team created in American Corner Pavlodar. We share a passion for space exploration, technology, and real-world problem solving. Our interests programming engineering data analysis software development Our goal is to develop an innovative, practical solution using resources from NASA. We’re looking for creative and driven teammates with experience in coding, web development in general, visualizing data, UI/UX design and space science.
summary:
At the Moon’s south pole a spot that looks absolutely promising on the map can in fact be a very difficult place to work in in the real world. The Sun is very low, there are long shadows all over the place and Earth isn't always up above the local horizon. Our intention was to make those constantly changing conditions a lot easier to deal with rather than having to go through the long ephemeris tables.



We built LunarSight which is an interactive web app that takes the NASA JPL Horizons Sun and Earth data and turns it into timelines, direction diagrams and side by side location comparisons. We then built Solar Rover Planner which takes the NASA published traverse station coordinates and the LOLA derived terrain imagery and looks at the effect of changing geometric visibility on a conceptual rover traverse.



Users can select a location and time, view the azimuth and elevation and go through a rover simulation all in one go. LunarSight is a prototype for learning and initial mission analysis only and is not a landing safety or autonomous navigation system. It has no model of local terrain shadows, no communication link budget and no verified traversable paths.
details:
The Problem

The Moon's South Pole is a promising destination for future lunar missions, but exploring it comes with some unusual challenges. The Sun stays close to the horizon, and even small changes in location or time can make a significant difference in visibility. For missions that depend on solar power and reliable communication with Earth, understanding these conditions is essential.

This led us to a question: what if we could make these complex conditions easier to understand, explore, and visualize?

Our Solution

We created LunarSight, an interactive web application that helps users explore how the positions of the Sun and Earth change when viewed from different locations on the Moon.

Astronomical data can be difficult to interpret, especially when it comes in the form of large tables of coordinates and timestamps. We wanted to turn that information into something people could actually interact with.

LunarSight brings together scientific calculations, interactive graphs, direction diagrams, and a simulated lunar rover mission.

The application consists of three main features.

Mission Control is where users can select a location on the Moon and a period of time to investigate. It shows how the Sun's and Earth's azimuth and elevation change over time, making it possible to identify periods when both are above the ideal horizon.

Site Comparison allows users to examine two lunar locations side by side over the same time period. This helps reveal how much visibility conditions can differ between potential mission sites.

Solar Rover Planner is something we decided to build beyond the original challenge requirements. Using published NASA traverse-station coordinates from the Shackleton–de Gerlache region and a georeferenced terrain map, we created a simulation where users can follow a rover's movement across the lunar surface.

As the rover moves, its position, route information, and astronomical conditions update together along a shared UTC timeline. This allows users to see how the mission develops rather than looking at separate sets of data.

How We Built It

We built LunarSight using Python and Streamlit, which allowed us to develop an interactive web application without needing a large infrastructure.

The scientific data comes from NASA's JPL Horizons API. Our backend requests observer ephemerides, validates the responses, and processes the resulting time-series data before displaying it to users.

We use Pandas to organize and process the data and Plotly to create interactive charts that users can explore directly.

The Solar Rover Planner required a different approach. We developed a separate routing module that represents lunar stations as nodes in a graph, with possible movements between them assigned estimated travel costs.

We implemented two planning modes. Visibility Optimization considers the geometric visibility of the Sun and Earth alongside travel-time constraints when evaluating possible movements. Continuous Exploration follows a conceptual route to demonstrate how a longer rover journey could be visualized.

One challenge was keeping the rover animation and astronomical data synchronized. To solve this, we built a browser-side JavaScript component that updates the rover's position and mission timeline smoothly, without forcing Streamlit to rerun the Python application for every animation frame.

For the terrain map, we used elevation data from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA). We processed the data into a lightweight hillshade so that users could explore the lunar landscape without loading an unnecessarily large dataset.

We also implemented ephemeris caching, local demonstration data, automated tests, and deployment through Streamlit Community Cloud.

What Makes Our Approach Different

From the beginning, we didn't want LunarSight to be just another tool that calculates astronomical coordinates.

We wanted users to understand what those numbers actually mean.

The part we're most excited about is the connection between location, time, and movement. Instead of studying separate charts or tables, users can move through a mission timeline and watch the rover change position while the corresponding visibility conditions update.

We also tried to make the experience accessible. You shouldn't need to know how to work with astronomical APIs or interpret raw ephemeris data to start exploring the Moon.

At the same time, we wanted to keep the scientific foundation of the application transparent, so users can understand what the calculations represent and where their limitations begin.

Impact and Future Development

We see LunarSight as both an educational tool and an early step toward more advanced lunar mission-planning software.

It can help students, space enthusiasts, and researchers explore how astronomical conditions vary across the lunar surface and why those differences matter when thinking about future missions.

Of course, there are things our current prototype cannot do yet.

Right now, LunarSight evaluates geometric visibility using an ideal horizon. It doesn't account for shadows caused by nearby terrain, calculate complete communication link budgets, simulate rover battery levels, or guarantee that a proposed route would be safe to drive.

These are important limitations, especially in a region as challenging as the lunar South Pole.

Our next steps would be to incorporate terrain-aware horizon calculations, build more realistic energy and communication models, and introduce path planning that considers the actual lunar terrain.

For us, LunarSight is not a finished mission-planning system. It's a starting point.

We hope it can grow into a more capable platform, one that other developers, students, and researchers can experiment with, improve, and build upon.

Ultimately, our goal is simple: make the challenges of exploring the Moon easier to see, understand, and investigate.
